title: Recursion
body:
[[Recursion]]
#1633-2631 

---

A [[Function]] that calls itself. Introduced at the very end of the course, and the reason it
works is the call stack.

Every recursive function needs two things, and missing either one is fatal:

1. A **base case** that returns without recursing.
2. A **recursive case** that calls itself on a strictly *smaller* problem.

```c++
int factorial(int n) {
	if (n <= 1) return 1;          // base case
	return n * factorial(n - 1);   // smaller every time
}
```

Miss the base case, or fail to shrink the problem, and the calls never stop. That is not an
[[Infinite loop]]; it is a **stack overflow**, because each call pushes a new frame and
nothing pops. See [[Stack and Heap]] and [[Runtime Errors]].

## Why it works

Nothing magic happens. Each call gets its own frame on the stack with its own copy of `n`,
its own locals, and the address to return to, exactly as [[Call by value]] and
[[Variable Lifetime]] already describe. Five calls deep there are five independent `n`s. The
frames unwind in reverse order as each `return` fires, which is why the multiplications in
`factorial` happen on the way *back up*. [[Subroutines]] in [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] shows the
actual `jsr` / `rts` and the stack pointer doing this.

## Where it earns its keep

Anything defined in terms of a smaller version of itself, which in this course means
[[Linked Structure]]s. Walking a [[Linked List]] recursively is "handle this [[Node]], then
handle the rest", and printing the list backwards is three lines recursively and genuinely
awkward with a loop:

```c++
void print_backwards(Node* p) {
	if (p == NULL) return;
	print_backwards(p->next);
	cout << p->data << " ";
}
```

[[GCD and LCM|Euclid's algorithm]] is the other natural fit. `factorial` and Fibonacci are the
teaching examples and are both better as loops; naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes the same
values exponentially many times, which is [[Time Complexity]]'s problem in
[[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]], along with [[Tree]] traversal and [[Merge Sort]], where recursion
stops being a curiosity.

Any recursion can be written as a loop and any loop as recursion. Use whichever makes the code
say what you mean.

Recursion and [[Proof By Induction]] are the same idea pointed in opposite directions: the
base case of the function is the base case of the proof, and the recursive call is the
inductive hypothesis. If you want to argue that a recursive function is correct, structural
[[Induction]] is the tool, and it is set up in [[DISCRETE MATH]].
